title: Protected measurements for protected superconducting qubits
authors: Xanda C Kolesnikow, Thomas B Smith, Andrew C Doherty
abstract: Protected superconducting qubits such as the $0$-$π$ qubit promise to substantially suppress error rates, facilitating fault-tolerant quantum computing with fewer qubits. Measuring these qubits is challenging due to their protected nature, and thus far no concrete proposal exists for how to measure them without breaking their protection. Here we show how to perform protected measurements of the $0$-$π$ qubit in two orthogonal bases. The protection of these measurements is facilitated by their quantum non-demolition nature, allowing faults on ancillary measurement qubits to be tolerated. As experimental progress pushes protected qubits further into the low error-rate regime, our techniques will be crucial for fault-tolerant universal control.
summary: This paper details methods to perform fault-tolerant measurements on protected $0-\pi$ superconducting qubits. By leveraging QND techniques and coupling the qubit state to auxiliary modes, the authors achieve measurement protocols for both Z and X bases. These results are crucial for realizing universal, error-corrected quantum computation in superconducting circuits.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing robust methods to measure protected superconducting qubits without destroying their inherent protection mechanisms, which is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: The authors successfully propose protocols for performing both Z and X basis measurements on the $0-\pi$ qubit that maintain its protected nature by utilizing Quantum Non-Demolition (QND) measurement principles.
method: Measurement relies on encoding logical information into auxiliary modes ($\zeta$ mode for Z, $	heta$ mode parity for X) and coupling this information to ancillary qubits via controlled gates like Echoed Controlled Displacement (ECD).
model_or_system: The system is the $0-\pi$ superconducting qubit, whose Hamiltonian involves multiple coupled Josephson junctions. The protection mechanism is linked to code structures, such as those related to rotor-GKP codes.
key_observables: Measurement error rates for both Z and X bases; identification of proximity to protected states ($\vert ar{0}angle$ or $\vert ar{1}angle$) via measurement outcomes.
important_parameters: Josephson coupling strengths ($E_J$), charging energies ($E_C$), ancillary qubit parameters, and control time scales (e.g., turn-off times $	au_{\downarrow}$).
main_assumptions: The protocols assume the ability to rapidly switch off Josephson junctions or treat certain modes classically for simplification in deriving error bounds.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Z measurement protocol using the $\zeta$ mode and ECD gates, and the X measurement by mapping information onto Cooper-pair parity of the $	heta$ mode. Later figures analyze how varying impedance affects these measured error rates.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general need for protected measurements to detailing specific protocols for Z and X bases on the $0-\pi$ qubit, followed by quantitative analysis showing the dependence of measurement errors on external parameters like impedance.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete theoretical blueprints for performing necessary diagnostic measurements (readout) on highly protected quantum hardware, directly addressing a major bottleneck in scaling up superconducting quantum processors.

(a) Z measurements identify anything closer to θ = 0 as a logical |¯0⟩(blue) and anything closer to θ = π as a logical |¯1⟩(orange). This can be implemented by measuring the direction of the current through a shunting Josephson junction. (b) X measurements identify any state with even Cooper-pair parity as a logical |¯+⟩(purple) and anything with odd Cooper-pair parity as a logical |¯−⟩(green). This can be implemented by measuring the voltage across the circuit.

FIG. 2. Measuring the 0-π qubit. (a) Z measurement. The protocol consists of smoothly turning on the shunting Josephson element (green) to prepare GKP states in the ζ mode of the 0-π qubit (red) that are entangled with its θ mode, then sharply turning off the Josephson element, returning the ζ mode to a linear oscillator. Through a series of Echoed Controlled Displacement (ECD) gates, the logical information in the GKP states is transferred to an ancillary qubit (cyan), which is then measured in a single shot via a readout resonator (gray).
